MEASURED 2026-08-13 by RUNNING reflow2 against flo2's committed export (`~/project/flo2/docs/design/flo2.json`, 106 nodes, graph_id `1a97fc1f1de4d5d2`, minted, stamp 0.27.0 against reflow2's 0.29.0). flo2 was NOT written to; the one designation experiment below was made on an in-memory copy.

═══ 1. COMPUTED PAIRING FINDS NOTHING BETWEEN TWO PROJECTS BUILT TO WORK TOGETHER ═══

`pair_designs`, both designs exactly as they stand:

    paired 0 · conflicts 10 · unmet_needs 5 · dead_surface 2 · candidates 1
    unclassified 2 ours / 1 theirs

flo2's `ifc:reflow2-design-api` ("reflow2 design tool surface") lands in DEAD SURFACE. Cause: both sides declare their half of the same contract as `published` — reflow2 publishes `ifc:mcp-tools`, flo2 publishes `ifc:reflow2-design-api` — and published↔published never pairs, which is the complementary-role rule working as designed. flo2 models that boundary from its own inside ("THE SEAM between the two halves of flo2"), which is locally defensible and makes cross-design pairing impossible.

═══ 2. 🛑🛑 FIXING THE ROLE DOES NOT FIX IT — THE NAME MATCHER RANKS THE WRONG ANSWER HIGHER ═══

Experiment, in memory only: flip flo2's `ifc:reflow2-design-api` to `both`. STILL 0 PAIRED, and the three considerations it produces are:

    81  ifc:graph-export  ↔ ifc:reflow2-design-api   WRONG, and ranked FIRST
    64  ifc:mcp-tools     ↔ ifc:reflow2-design-api   RIGHT, stuck in the candidate band (60-85)
    61  ifc:mcp-tools     ↔ ifc:model-provider-api   WRONG

⇒ **THE ONLY TRUE SEAM THESE TWO PROJECTS HAVE IS OUT-RANKED BY AN INCORRECT MATCH**, because "Design export document" and "reflow2 design tool surface" share the word *design*. WHAT PREVENTED A FALSE PAIR WAS THE ATTRIBUTE KEY, NOT THE NAMES: `medium` disagreed (`data` vs `REST`). Had flo2 said `data`, reflow2 would have confidently paired the wrong two boundaries — the failure `dec:idea-defined-pair-types-so-two-projects-combine-by-lookup` already recorded from the dynograph-foundation trial. Most of the 10 conflicts are the same noise: reflow2's `req-dyno-*` (`medium: library`) matching flo2's REST APIs at 77-83 on *-api* overlap alone.

⭐⭐ THIS IS THE EMPIRICAL CASE FOR OPTION C (`SPECIFIES`, where the content hash IS the agreement). It was argued theoretically on that node; here the name matcher is observed producing a wrong answer ABOVE the right one, on the only real seam available.

═══ 3. ✅ THE ASSERTED PAIR ANSWERS THE ACTUAL GOAL, AND IT IS A DIFFERENT TOOL ═══

`seam_report` with the pair supplied BY HAND — `ifc:mcp-tools` ↔ `ifc:reflow2-design-api`:

    agreed 3 · incompatible 0 · differs 0 · UNSTATED BY NOBODY 5

⇒ **THE TWO PROJECTS ARE COMPATIBLE AS FAR AS ANYTHING IS STATED, AND FIVE NAMED AXES STAND BETWEEN "roughly interfaces" AND "fully specified"**: `auth`, `transport_security`, `operations`, `error_model`, `payload_schema`.

🛑 AND REFLOW2 IS THE SILENT SIDE ON THE TWO THAT MATTER. flo2 states `auth: none` and `transport_security: tls`; reflow2's own PUBLISHED `ifc:mcp-tools` states NEITHER. The report's own wording: *"we assume `unstated`, they require `none` — the side that assumed less finds out in production"*. reflow2 has not specified its own published boundary, and only a cross-project check surfaced it.

📌 NOT EXAMINED, and it is named in the output rather than left implied: THE TYPES THAT CROSS the boundary (`con:pairing-stops-at-the-boundary`). Every axis above is a property OF a boundary; a struct travelling through one is invisible to the check.

═══ 4. TWO OPERATIONAL NOTES ═══

· `mirrors` on reflow2 returns **0**. The machinery for "I designed against your published surface, pinned at this version" is BUILT and has never been used on the one pair of projects that most obviously calls for it.
· The by-name CLI degraded to `pair_designs: tool not found` because a `--serve-shared` daemon (pid 892293) held the store lock — `fact:the-degraded-surfaces-diagnosis-never-reaches-a-by-name-caller` again, third sighting. THE CURE THAT WORKED: spawn the client with `--shared` so it attaches through the daemon instead of taking the lock.
